analysis.one_liner: Tightens FDA oversight of cosmetics safety, bans several toxic ingredients, and requires full ingredient disclosure.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or any floor action before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would give the Food and Drug Administration real power over cosmetics for the first time in decades: a firm safety standard, an annual fee on larger companies, mandatory recall authority for unsafe products, full ingredient labeling including fragrance chemicals, mandatory reporting of serious health reactions, and an immediate ban on a list of ingredients linked to cancer, hormone disruption, and reproductive harm. It would also ban cosmetic animal testing, require safety data sheets for salon workers in multiple languages, and fund research on chemical exposures affecting women and girls of color.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary consumers who use cosmetics daily, plus salon and nail-salon workers who breathe and handle these products all day at far higher exposure levels than customers. Women and girls of color, who are marketed products with more harmful chemicals, would gain from targeted research and safer formulations. Small cosmetic makers would benefit from exemptions from fees and registration, plus federal technical support.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers, salon workers, women of color

how_it_helps.text: Immediately bans a list of ingredients linked to cancer, reproductive harm, or hormone disruption, including certain phthalates, formaldehyde-releasing preservatives, parabens, lead compounds, triclosan, and toluene, and requires manufacturers to reformulate within a year [S3].

Establishes a safety standard of 'reasonable certainty of no harm' considering cumulative and low-dose exposure, and lets the FDA force a recall of an unsafe cosmetic rather than asking companies to recall voluntarily [S3].

Requires full ingredient labels, including hazardous fragrance ingredients and contaminants that companies currently can hide as trade secrets, on packages, brand websites, and online store listings [S3].

Requires salon and spa employers to keep material safety data sheets available to employees, translated into English, Spanish, Vietnamese, Chinese, and Korean, recognizing that salon workers are a highly exposed population [S3].
Bans animal testing for cosmetics and funds research into safer alternatives and into the health effects of cosmetics marketed to women and girls of color [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Cosmetics and personal care manufacturers, ingredient suppliers, and fragrance makers, who would pay annual registration fees (only companies above $5 million in sales), reformulate products, run contaminant testing, disclose fragrance ingredients they have kept as trade secrets, and comply with mandatory recall and adverse-event reporting. Some added compliance costs would likely reach consumers in prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large cosmetics makers and fragrance suppliers

drawbacks.text: The bill deems a long list of ingredients banned immediately on enactment, without waiting for the FDA's regulatory process; some, like the sunscreen filters benzophenone-3 and octinoxate, are widely used, so removal could disrupt product lines and raise costs before substitutes are fully available [S3].

The 'one in a million risk' safety benchmark is far stricter than most existing chemical standards, which would force extensive reformulation and testing industry-wide and likely push up consumer prices [S3].

Compliance paperwork, testing, and reformulation requirements fall heaviest on mid-sized brands; the microbusiness exemption (under $1 million in sales) leaves companies just above that line with most of the burden and none of the scale to absorb it [S3].
Annual fees, an FDA database, audits, and grants for safer-chemicals research all require appropriations, so the program's strength would depend on Congress actually funding it [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health benefit is real but slow-moving: today's cosmetics law essentially trusts companies to self-certify safety, and this bill would replace that with testing, disclosure, and recall power. The costs are genuine — reformulation, fees, and some price increases — but they fall mainly on larger companies, with deliberate carve-outs for microbusinesses and salon operators. The immediate ban list is the sharpest edge of the bill and the most likely source of disruption, though products with those ingredients would have to be replaced rather than lost. On balance the design tries to protect the public while sparing small sellers, and its main defect is administrative: it asks the FDA to do a great deal of new work that Congress would have to fund.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and its Health Subcommittee, and it sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Representative Jan Schakowsky introduced the bill on September 12, 2019 with 17 original cosponsors, all Democrats [S3].
It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Education and Labor Committee the day it was introduced, and the next day to the Health Subcommittee [S5].
No further action was ever taken; the bill received no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote, and was not carried over into the next Congress [S5].
It attracted 41 cosponsors over its lifetime, all House Democrats — about one in five of the Democratic caucus — but never reached the floor [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large cosmetics and fragrance companies kept the status quo: no registration fees, no mandatory recalls, no disclosure of fragrance chemicals, and no reformulation mandates.

sides.party_line_note: All 42 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican signed on; the record shows no floor vote, so no roll-call split exists.

industries.note: The bill would impose annual fees on companies over $5 million in sales, ban a list of common ingredients outright, require reformulation within a year of any listing, and give the FDA mandatory recall power. It would also end the current system in which companies essentially self-certify that their products are safe.

Fragrance formulas are today protected as trade secrets; the bill would require hazardous fragrance ingredients, allergens, and contaminants above set thresholds to appear on labels and websites, and states that anything required on a label is not a trade secret.

Companies under $1 million in sales are exempt from registration and fees, no fees apply under $5 million in sales, and the FDA must provide technical support to small businesses. This shields independent and artisanal makers from the compliance costs falling on larger rivals.

Animal testing to develop cosmetics would be unlawful immediately on enactment, with a narrow exception when safety cannot be established by validated non-animal methods, and grants would fund development of non-animal tests.
